description: We are NOVEX, a team of curious and passionate innovators driven by science, technology, and space exploration. We aim to transform creative ideas into meaningful solutions by using data, collaboration, and innovative thinking to tackle real-world challenges. Together, we aspire to explore new possibilities and make a positive impact through technology and discovery
summary:
We developed a game prototype called Satellite Designer using Godot. It is a resource-management game and runs on desktop(windows), web and android in the compatibility renderer at 1280x720. Everything is build from procedural shapes and sounds with no external assets. Players will play either as a solo or a team of 4 to design a satellite from one of three missions which are Earth Climate Change, Weather Tracker or Lunar Survey. Players choose parts, watch a live dashboard of mass, cost, power, data, science and lifetime, then launch and survive random events such as solar flares or wheel failures. A report explains why the mission succeeded or failed.

It addresses the challenge by turning real mission-design trade-offs into play. Solo and Team modes (four roles with sign-offs) show how engineers share responsibility. Easy, Normal and Hard settings control difficulty. A How to play popup and an adaptive coach bar guide new players.

It matters because it makes systems engineering approachable and teaches margins, constraints and teamwork.
details:
Satellite Designer is a solo or co-op resource-management game. You pick a difficulty and one of three missions (like Earth Climate Watch or Lunar Survey), then build a satellite by configuring key subsystems like solar panels, instruments, orbit, shielding, and a spare wheel. A live dashboard tracks mass, cost, power, data, science, and lifetime, flashing green as gates pass.
On launch, 3 random space events trigger (4 on Hard)—such as a solar flare, ground outage, or wheel glitch—that eat into your margins or destroy an unprotected craft. A short flight animation plays, followed by a report with your score, 1–3 stars, a timeline, and a plain-language "Why it happened" explanation. Best scores save per mission. All logic lives in one autoload script (GameState), while UI screens only read from it.

Benefits & Intended Impacts
•Teaches systems engineering: Shows how parts trade mass, cost, and power, and why margins matter when events hit.
•Learn from failures: Reports explain issues in plain language.
•Real teamwork: Team mode (Systems, Power, Payload, Ops) mirrors how real teams split work and sign off.
•Beginner-friendly: A tutorial and coach bar make it playable with zero prior knowledge, aiming to spark interest in space mission design.

Tools & Technology
•Godot 4 (GDScript, Compatibility renderer, 1280x720) for desktop/web export, using UI Controls, Tweens, CPUParticles2D, ConfigFile, AudioStreamGenerator, and AudioStreamWAV (looping drone).
•Python to verify every mission/difficulty is winnable; Claude to help write code; Godot editor to run and test.

Creativity
•100% procedural: No external assets—just a geometric satellite that grows as you pick parts, a twinkling starfield, generated chimes, and a drone.
•Risk vs. reward: Shielding and spare wheels cost mass and money, but prevent fatal failures.
•Co-op constraints & adaptive UI: Role limits force team coordination, while a coach bar updates advice based on your live design.

Factors Considered
•Balance & accessibility: Python-verified winnable builds, Hard mode requiring protection, an Easy mode (fewer parts, no fatal events), and a how-to-play popup with diagrams and hints.
•Performance & transparency: Asset-free web export runs in browsers (including phones), with simplified gameplay numbers instead of real NASA data.
•Known limits: Desktop-sized UI looks small on phones, and browser audio starts only after a click.
